en: Preface to the *Conglin Gonglun* (Public Discourse on Forest Monasteries):
The bells and drums are not the essence of music, yet the instruments cannot be discarded; formal discourse is not the essence of the Way, yet speech cannot be eliminated.
If one preserves the instruments while forgetting their essence, this is why music becomes lost; if one establishes words while forgetting their essence, the Way [becomes lost].
This is why they were lost. Yet, without the instruments, there was no way to hear the "Nine Shao" music;

without the words, there was no way to manifest the Way of the Single Thread. Only by tuning the instruments to the Mean and Harmony is music perfected; only by speaking with Great Impartiality are words realized.

The Way is luminous. Nan-dang, the Elder Ān, was my upright friend. Since I first received his instruction more than two decades ago, I have observed that he is a man of profound character and a personification of benevolence.
He is broad-minded and nurtures all things; in his daily life, he is tranquil and simple, appearing humble and almost unable to speak.
Yet, when expounding the Dharma, he rebukes even the Buddhas and patriarchs, and in his discourse, he is incisive and unyielding.
From ancient times to the present, public discourse has amounted to over ten thousand words; summarizing their general tenor, this work is not something created out of thin air.

I have weighed its principles with care, ensuring that no deficiency remains unaddressed, while also investigating its instances of censure and exposure, as well as its attempts to sweep away distinctions between right and wrong.

I have scrutinized the errors in his handling of the *Jin'gen* (Golden Root) texts with great care, deeply fearing that later students might follow and be deluded by his theories, leading them into a web of absurdity and causing them to abandon the true path.
Yet, when one examines his ultimate fairness and correctness, he enters the realm of the sages with ease. His clarity rivals that of the sun and moon;
his greatness matches that of heaven and earth; his profundity equals that of the rivers and seas; and his loftiness is on par with the mountains and peaks. It is vast indeed.
Vast and sublime! That which has its root is thus. Alas! When harmonious qi permeates and mingles, and the gracious breeze flows freely, there is no branch that does not sprout.
Let students not allow themselves to remain empty. Written by the Master of Yu-kuei-yen, Zonghui, in the final spring of the Jiyou year of the Chunxi era.
*Conglin Gonglun* (Public Discourse on the Forest Monasteries), composed by An Huibin.
In the *Sengbao Zhuan*, the eulogy for Master Qi Chan says: "Long ago, there was a monk who asked Zhaozhou, 'What is the Patriarch’s West [Gate]?'..."
Regarding the intent behind [the Master’s] coming, he replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. Furthermore, he followed this by admonishing him, saying:
"If you are willing to accept what I have said, then I have failed you; if you are not willing to accept what I have said, then I have not failed you.
Those who are ignorant have truncated this, thereby failing to preserve the full intent of the ancients; the harm caused is profound. Therefore, I have recorded it here in its entirety.
The Public Critique (*Gōron*) says: "From where did Juefan obtain this statement? Therefore, I have recorded it here as well. It further states:
"Those who are ignorant plagiarize [the words of others], causing the intent of the ancients to remain incomplete; the harm is truly great. Does this harm nature, or does it harm destiny?"
Does this harm the Way or its virtue? Does it harm human affairs or social transformation? I hope you will clarify this for me, so that future generations may not be confused by it.
It is like when a monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?"
The answer was, “The cypress tree in the courtyard. How could the intention of the ancients not be considered extremely harmful?
For instance, Fayan asked Chan Master Jue of Guangxiao Temple in Yangzhou, “Where have you recently come from? He replied, “From Zhaozhou.
Fayan said, “I have heard that Zhaozhou has the ‘cypress tree’ story; is this true? Jue said, “No. Fayan remarked, “The monastic community is flourishing!”
How can you claim that this was not said? Jue said, "My late master truly did not say these words. Preceptor, do not slander my late master.
When Guangxiao replied in such a manner, does he not cause the intent of the ancients to be rendered largely incomplete?
If Ji-yin has no blood under his skin, that is one thing; but if he does, upon hearing this, would he not feel shame and remorse? If Zhaozhou had actually [said those things] at that time...
There are expressions concerning "guilt" and "innocence. If the ignorant were to eliminate them, how could their meaning remain complete?
To add what does not exist through mere conjecture is like drawing legs on a snake. Alas! Once the tongue has spoken, even four horses cannot overtake it.
Liang Su composed the "Discourse on the Dharma-Gates of Tiantai. Its summary states: "Among people today, those with correct faith are rare.

Those who wander through the gates of Chan sometimes employ the teaching that there is neither Buddha nor Dharma, and neither sin nor merit, to transform those of middling capacity and below, as well as those who pursue the throngs of desire and those within the ranks of the gentry.
They consider these words to be ultimate and do not oppose them."
Thus, those who follow his path are like moths rushing toward a bright candle or clods of earth falling into a deep valley;
they do not realize that they are being driven to scorching ruin and are unable to escape themselves. Though he intended to benefit them, he has in fact harmed them.
This is identical in its nature to the harm wrought by the various māras and non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Alas! How can Su have been so lacking in reflection as to rashly utter such [words]?
Regarding this, I, Su, say that those who possess "correct faith" know only the name of correct faith, yet do not know the reality of correct faith.
To enter the reality of correct faith is to find neither Buddha nor Dharma; what, then, can be called sin or virtue? Furthermore, I, Su, cite a sutra which says:
"Opening the gate of expedient means, he reveals the mark of ultimate truth. This is illustrated by the metaphor of the various rivers flowing into the sea, and is designated as...
Regarding the "Gate of Non-duality," your disciples know only the words for citing the sutras, yet they do not understand where the sutras lead.
If one clearly awakens to the true mark and the Dharma-gate of non-duality, it is a time when there is neither Buddha nor Dharma, and neither sin nor merit.
Therefore, the sutra says: "If one contemplates in this way, it is called right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called false contemplation."
From the perspective of Master Su, he would not have had to wait for the candlelight to reach him before his seat was already scorched.
The *Dongshan Shiyi* states that Yuanjian said to the Patriarch, "The elder Touzi Qing is here on this mountain;
at Huishengyan, he has attained a point of entry into the old monk’s teaching. He then entrusted the Great Yang school's fundamental tenets to him. One day, he paid his respects and said: "Great..."
Yang Zongyi said, "I have already received the transmission of the Master’s [Yangshan] school. May I hear the essential tenets of Linji?
Yuanjian replied, "By my final testament, I have transmitted the bloodline of Dongshan. As for the essential tenets of Linji, you have not even dreamed of them.
When the Patriarch [Yang Zongyi] related this matter to Liaoheng, Touzi’s *Chuan* (Record) states: "When Chan Master Yuanjian Yuan retired from his seat..."
At Huisheng Rock, Huiyuan had long dreamed of obtaining a fine hawk and raising it. Upon waking, Qing arrived just as he had envisioned;
Huiyuan took this as an auspicious omen and treated him with special courtesy. After three years, Huiyuan asked:

"When an outsider questioned the Buddha, asking whether he would speak of existence or non-existence, and the World-Honored One remained silent—how do you understand this? As Qing was about to offer a reply, Huiyuan [struck him].
Suddenly, [Zhaozhou] covered his mouth with his hand. Thereupon, Qingming attained awakening. He bowed and rose. Yuan said, "Have you attained a wondrous realization of the profound mechanism?

Qing replied, "Even if there were a wondrous realization, it must be spat out. At that time, Attendant Zishi was standing nearby and said, "Today Qing Huayan is like one who has broken a feverish sweat.
Qing looked back and said, "Shut your dog’s mouth! Do not chatter further!"
I immediately vomited. [Linji] said, "As for the essential tenets of Linji, you have not even dreamed of them. The Patriarch spoke these words for the sake of Liaoheng;
he was pointing to a concrete fact, meaning that Touzi had indeed never dreamed of the essential tenets of Linji.
Touzi attained awakening and gained entry in his time; did he enter the school of Linji, or the school of Dongshan?
Did he awaken to the school of Dongshan, or did he awaken to the school of Linji? If one has neither awakened nor entered, then that is that.
But since he has awakened and entered, what further discussion can there be? Indeed, throughout antiquity and the present, the Way is not two; the sages have no dual minds. Since he has awakened—
Once you have entered [the Way], why dwell on the interval between Linji and Dongshan? What is now called the "Five Houses" refers merely to their gateways and courtyards;
how could their Way itself be different? If there were indeed such differences, they would be mere heterodoxies—how could they be the Way of our ancestors, Bodhidharma?
Furthermore, consider how Touzi, after his awakening, engaged in a dialogue with Fushan. Fushan said to him: "You..."
"Have you attained a wondrous realization of the profound mechanism? Touzi was able to say: "Even if you have a wondrous realization, you must spit it out.
Attendant Zishou said, "Today Qing Huayan is like one who has obtained a medicinal sweat after being ill. Touzi looked back and said, "Shut that dog’s mouth!"
"You speak on and on; I shall immediately vomit. At that time, did Touzi employ the tenets of Dongshan, or the tenets of Linji?
Shiyi then disseminated this as a worldly convention, taking it to be the literal truth, saying: "The Patriarch understood for the sake of Lianghen and spoke these words.
Alas! Those whom the ancients called men of immeasurable greatness have, in fact, been turned around by the flow of mere words.
It is further said: "One must not speak of dreams in the presence of a fool. I have examined this passage once more;
it does not appear to be the handwriting of Daoxuan (Shiyi). I fear that later generations, driven by their own blood-and-qi impulses, have attributed this to Daoxuan, claiming he spoke these words.
Ouyang Xiu’s "Original Discourse on Buddhism" states: "The Buddhist Dharma has been a plague to this Middle Kingdom for over a thousand years.

Among those in the world who are eminent, unconfused, and possessed of power, there are none who do not wish to eliminate it. It has already been eliminated, yet it gathers once more; it is attacked and briefly defeated, yet it becomes even firmer;
it is suppressed before being extinguished, yet it blazes even more fiercely. Thus, it has reached a state where nothing can be done. This is the public consensus.
He said: "Alas! That which endures in this world cannot tolerate falsehood. If such falsehood does not perish today, it will surely perish tomorrow.
The Buddha-dharma has been present in China for no small number of days; though attacked, it has not been broken but has become ever firmer;
though struck down, it has not been extinguished but has become ever more blazing. Knowing that there is nothing to be done, how can one not reflect deeply upon this?"

Is it because they are false yet appear true? I, Meng, have reflected on this further. In examining any discourse, one should grasp its underlying intent rather than seeking it through the literal facts.
As Mencius said: "To meet the will with one's own intention is to attain it. What Ou-yang discussed was not intended to exclude Buddhism;
rather, he sought to strengthen the Way of the Confucians. He stated that ritual and righteousness constitute the very foundation for surpassing Buddhism. Thus spoke Han Yu.
He said: "Furthermore, there is a reason why I do not assist the followers of Śākyamuni but instead refute them;
this is also out of concern for the gradual decline of the Confucian Way. Both Han Yu and Ouyang Xiu were great Confucian scholars.
Their refutation and dismantling of [Buddhism] actually serves to stimulate and exalt our own Buddhist Way—how could it be called a minor contribution?"
Chan Master Yongjia’s verse says: "If one uses knowledge to know stillness, this is not a knowledge devoid of conditions.
It is like a hand grasping a *cintāmaṇi* jewel; it is not that the hand lacks the jewel. If one uses self-knowledge to know, this too is not a knowledge devoid of conditions.

It is like a hand naturally forming a fist; it is not that the hand is not a fist. Furthermore, one does not use knowledge to know stillness, nor does one use self-knowledge to know; yet it cannot be said to be non-existent."
It is known because its nature is luminously clear; thus it is not the same as wood or stone.
Just as a hand does not grasp an object and likewise does not form a fist of its own accord, yet one cannot say it is handless because the hand remains at ease, it is not the same as a rabbit’s horn.

Juefan said: "Yongjia spoke only of the ailments that arise after awakening. A public commentary states: "If one has not awakened, that is that. But once one has awakened, how could there still be any ailment?"
This specifically refers to the gate of awakening for practitioners; it does not speak of the maladies that arise after awakening. Juefan further said:
"How could the principles of the world be exhausted by a single word? Gonglun said: "The principles of the world are exhausted without even waiting for a single word."
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space; it is neither internal nor external, yet exists everywhere. It is further said:
"There is nothing in all the world that is not empty space. Because one takes such things as tiles and stones as the objects contrasted with empty space, it is said, "in contrast to empty space.
Hong Juefan’s brief eulogy for Chan Master Yuchi of Fachang states: "The place where he dwelt was a desolate village of ruined..."

In the monastery, when he struck the drum with all his might to preach Chan to the eighteen clay images, although he did not reach the level of having a multitude like the True Single Disciples (Shenxiu and Huineng), he was nonetheless slightly superior to Master Sheng’s gathering of stones. Alas! Clay is an image;
stone is also an image. An image and an image are like space confronting space; how can they be distinguished by deluded views?
Comparing their strengths and weaknesses, the junior disciples were mistaken.
When Chan Master Sixin Xin visited Chan Master Baoguo at Huanglong, his eloquence was unimpeded.
Baoguo said, "Is this all your skill? Xin was flustered and unable to proceed further; he was subsequently rebuked and hurried out, remaining silent.
The "Sitting on the Mat" story: When the administrative official struck the practitioner, he suddenly attained great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of the staff.

Old Man Qing of Zhufeng Hermitage praised this, saying: "I have read the account of Sishin’s gateway to enlightenment; it is truly what is meant by 'a thirsty horse rushing to a spring' or 'an enraged lion tearing through rock.
Yet, when Sishin attained great enlightenment upon hearing the sound of the staff, both subject and object were forgotten, and the capacity and the object were simultaneously obliterated."
Even if one were to attempt to describe it using empty space as an analogy, it could not be grasped; only Buddha after Buddha can exhaustively fathom it.
To use an aged, thirsty horse or a wrathful lion as metaphors is like a blind man feeling an elephant—it is not far from the mark? Indeed, how remote it is!
Master Yichuan said: "The Buddhist teaching regarding the 'obstruction of principle' (li-zhang) means that once one has clarified this principle, yet still clings to it;
for this reason, it is called an obstruction. This is a misunderstanding of the word 'principle. In all under heaven, there is only this single principle.
Once this principle is clarified, what further obstruction could there be? If one takes principle itself to be an obstruction, then one is already at odds with principle."
Second. The Public Discourse states: Principle is fundamentally already manifest; to give rise to a single thought to clarify it is already to create an obstruction, let alone to cling to it.
Confucius said, "The worthy exceed [the mark], while the unworthy fall short. This precisely refers to the two obstructions of principle and phenomena.
If one were to boast of oneself and disparage others, claiming "I am right and they are wrong," how could this be anything less than making oneself and principle into two separate things?
*Lengzhai Yehua* (Cold Studio Night Talks) states: When Lord Shu was residing at Mount Zhong, he and Yu Xiulao of Jinhua went to the home of an old acquaintance for a drink.
After they had finished drinking, they walked to a water pavilion and observed several yellow and white objects, which appeared to be food vessels, lying among the sand by the water’s edge.
[This] matter: [It was discovered that] the officials and soldiers had stolen it. Therefore, he sent someone to question those in charge of it.
It turned out that some children had just gathered there to eat dates and chestnuts; having finished eating them, they had discarded them and left.

The King said to Master Xiùlǎo, "If a man wishes to undertake great affairs and experience wealth and honor, he must be able to act like this group of children. He further said, "I shall simply use Xuefeng..."
A single phrase made him a prime minister. Zhu Shiying said, "I wish to hear Xuefeng’s words. Wang said, "This old man once said to the assembly: 'What is it? Ah!
When the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence; when the wise see it, they call it wisdom.
Upon hearing this, King Shu regarded the world's precious goods as being like lightning, dew, a mirage, or flowers in the sky. Thus he [attained realization].

To turn one's private residence into a monastery is merely to follow these words. Jiyin (Zhu Xi) cites various anecdotes and compiles them into a formal record to be disseminated among the world’s archives;
through this, it is clearly evident that Jiyin never truly realized the essential purport of the Chan school.
His composition of admonitory remarks alongside Emperor Shu (Su Shi) can be understood with perfect clarity. As the *I Ching* says: "The blind can see; the lame can walk. Jiyin...
Is this not what is meant?

Let the scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant each attend to their respective duties. Should they happen to act in contradiction or confusion, then round wood placed in a square hole will invariably disrupt the laws of the world;

the followers of Śākyamuni, in particular, ought not to involve themselves in such matters. Having shaved their hair and donned the monastic robes, they become those who stand outside the mundane world, taking only what is necessary for sustenance.

Regarding the practice of receiving robes for one’s livelihood, the rules for the long precepts (*dīrgha-śīla*) state that one must not involve oneself in worldly affairs, act as a messenger, or cultivate friendships with persons of high status.
Yet today there are those who improperly join their ranks, addressing their patrons (*dānapati*) as "Lord of Grace" (*enfu*), being even more sycophantic and insincere than before.

Among people, there are those who receive a thousand pieces of gold daily, and there are those who have been nurtured from the egg until they possess wings; may you plan for the well-being of your descendants, generation after generation.
As for the subsequent plans deemed appropriate, whether they were designated as such or not, these were instances of overstepping one's station.

Yet, there were those who manifested the physical marks of a *brahman*, constructed Buddhist monasteries, and provided them with the four requisites; this was because their profound faith aspired to the Dharma and served as external protection for the religious teachings.
He may be called a great *dānapati* and a master of merit.

Chan Master Cui of Mount He in Huzhou was a native of Min. He was stern and possessed a sense of discipline; if a student came to visit him and lacked even the slightest courtesy, he would immediately scold them and instruct them.
Yet, his own conduct toward others was also generous. One day, while accompanying several high-ranking officials as they ascended a path...
At Changshan, he saw a painting of the cycle of transmigration within the three realms on the wall and asked the Master, "What is the meaning of this?
The Master replied, "It is not only in the Buddhist scriptures that this is spoken of; even Confucius has explained it in detail. The monk asked, "What did he say? The Master said, "Confucius said:
'Natures are nearly the same, but habits lead them far apart. The official, placing his palms together, nodded in agreement.
Zhouzi’s *Tongshu* says: "Sincerity (*cheng*) is the foundation of the sage. How great is the Great Primordial of Qian! All things derive their beginning from it; this is the source of sincerity.
Through the transformations of the Way of Qian, each thing rectifies its nature and destiny; therein does sincerity establish itself. It is pure, unadulterated, and supremely good."
Therefore it is said: "The alternation of Yin and Yang is what we call the Way (Dào). That which continues it is goodness (shàn); that which completes it is nature (xìng).

'Originality and Pervasiveness' (yuán-hēng) is the penetration of sincerity (chéng); 'Advantageousness and Constancy' (lì-zhēn) is the return of sincerity. How great is the *Yī*! It is the source of nature and destiny! The Public Commentary states:
When the Great Ultimate (tài-jí) moves, the Three Powers (sān-cái) are complete. Yet, sincerity, the *Yī*, and nature are one and the same entity.
These are different names; they do not exist in dependence upon a sequence. "One Yin and one Yang are called the Way.
It cannot be seen, yet that which is seen is its function. It is like clouds: without turning one's gaze, they are everywhere.
If it were to exist in dependence upon a sequence, would it not be both partial and laborious? [The Master] said: Both Yuan and Li are incorrect.
The *Tongshu* says: "The sage aspires to Heaven; the worthy aspires to the sage; the scholar aspires to the worthy. The *Gonglun* says: "Confucius was one who studied the Duke of Zhou.
Whether walking, staying, eating, or resting—even in his dreams—he saw the Duke of Zhou before him.

Once he had attained the state of the Duke of Zhou, Confucius was Zhou, and Zhou was Confucius. Therefore he said, 'I no longer dream of seeing the Duke of Zhou. The sage is Heaven; Heaven is the sage."
One is then a sage. Since one is already a sage, what more could one hope for? Heaven is the essence; the sage is the function. To say that the sage aspires to Heaven—I say this is not so.
During the Xīníng era, there was Master Héngqú, surnamed Zhāng and named Zǎi, who authored ten scrolls of a work titled *Zhèngméng*.

In it, his discussion on human nature (*xìng*) states: "That which unifies existence and non-existence, the void and the real, as a single entity is nature; that which cannot unify these is not one who has fully realized their nature.
Bǐchū Kějùn remarked: "Alas! To discuss nature in such a manner is merely the shadow and echo of the name of nature."
Furthermore, to never speak of the principle of self-attainment is what our school designates as "dead words," and what Lún Pián called "dregs. How could such [teachings] fully realize one's nature?
Mencius said: "The gentleman pursues profound cultivation through the Way, desiring that he attain it for himself.

If one does not take self-attainment as the criterion of verification, then the heterodox and the orthodox among the various schools of learning in the world will remain indistinguishable; how then [could there be true understanding]?
Is it not so? Master Cheng Yi said: "In the *Zhengmeng*, there are indeed some errors in Zhang Zai’s established doctrines.
Public opinion says: "To call it 'one thing' is already incorrect."
Honor and disgrace, gain and loss, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure follow these. Nothing brings greater honor than a decree from the sovereign;
nothing brings greater disgrace than punishment by law or execution. Should one encounter such things, the mind becomes blinded and its natural composure is lost.
Only those who have attained the Way and possess refined discernment remain tranquil. Yet, when our kindred encounter such circumstances, how ought they to respond?
Emperor Yingzong personally issued an imperial edict granting Chan Master Da’jue Lian the privilege of residing at any monastery in the empire as he pleased;
this was not to the master’s benefit. Later, when Dongpo composed the inscription for the Chenshui Pavilion, he sent a letter to inquire about it, saying:

"I have already completed the draft of the inscription for the Chenshui Pavilion. Being frail and having neglected my studies, I do not know whether it is fit to be engraved upon stone. I heard this from Canliao."

On the day the Chan Master departed from the capital, King Yeongmyo bestowed a handwritten edict. Its purport stated: "Regarding the phrase 'residing as abbot according to one's own nature,' I do not know for certain whether it is true or not;
I earnestly request that you record and show it to me. He wished to include this entire passage here, but Joak replied, "There is none."

Jué died. Subsequently, his book was found inside a chest. In the first year of the Daguān era, the Emperor bestowed a purple *kāṣāya* upon the Venerable Fúróng Kǎi and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dìngzhào.
Kǎi declined the honor and refused to accept the fame and profit.

The Governor of Kaifeng, Lǐ Xiàoshòu, was dispatched in person by the court to convey the imperial intent of honoring his virtue; however, Kǎi remained firm and would not change his mind. The Governor reported this in full detail.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor was enraged and ordered them to be handed over to the authorities. The officials said, "The Elder is withered and aged, and suffers from illness;

according to the law, he should be exempted from punishment and banished. Fajie replied, "In the past I had an illness, but now it has been cured. Thereupon, he donned lay robes and was sent to be registered in Zizhou. Alas!
These two great elders not only attained the depths of the Way, but truly grasped the essential character of a bhikṣu; they were worthy to be leaders.

Regarding this dharma: those who preside over it today rejoice with expressions of overflowing delight whenever they encounter a single instance of good fortune, manifesting an air of being unable to contain their joy;
yet should they fail, they wag their tails and beg for pity. Alas! As for the Great Awakened One and Fuyong, we have not seen them yet—do they no longer exist?
Who, then, are those who preside over the dharma?

The *Chànlín Sēngbǎo Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of the Chan Forest) serves to illuminate the Great Way of the former virtuous masters and to radiate their brilliance after their passing;
it is for this reason that the works titled *Jìchuán Dēng*, *Guǎngdēng*, and *Xùdēng* were composed. This book circulates like fire struck from a flint, present in every household.
However, the biographies therein are often exaggerated, and the eulogies frequently rely on conjecture, leading to errors that permeate later students. At the same time, various great [masters]...
The Elder Master has brought forth the ancient and the modern, illuminating them as clearly as the sun and moon, yet he offers not a single word of approval or disapproval.
Why is this? Is it that the good do not judge, or that those who judge are not good? Is it that his book is insufficient for judgment?
Or does the gentleman still harbor partiality? Perhaps he has indeed judged it, but I, Meng, have simply not seen it.
The Layman Zang, named Hong, was a native of Siming. Whenever he encountered a monk, he would invariably test him. One day, while sitting in a wine shop, a monk entered from outside to beg for alms.
He stood there for a long time, until the Layman suddenly called out in a stern voice, "Good! Good! Zang pushed aside the curtain and asked, "In what way are they good?
The monk pointed to the wine banner and said, "On the road there are flowers and also wine; one journey is shared."
They traveled for two stages. [The Master] said, "That is not it. Zang asked, "Where did you get this news? The monk said, "I bought it as before.
Zang said, "If that is so, then you are dragging along mud and water. The monk made a gesture of falling over and said, "Help me, old monk, and let us go back!"

Yichuan said: "The *Zhongyong* speaks of the Way; it requires only these four characters, 'no sound, no scent,' to encompass all the many words of the Buddhists such as 'neither yellow nor white, neither salty nor bitter.
Gonglun said: "The Way does not depend on the quantity of words.
It is like saying, 'When one's words fill the world, there is no fault in the mouth; when one's conduct fills the world, there is no resentment or malice.'"
Why is this? A monk asked the Great Master Yunmen, "What is the Eye of the True Dharma? Yunmen said, "Universal.
And why is this? To speak! To speak! How remote it is! How far-reaching it is!
Chan Master Puchu of Siming was a native of Min who possessed extensive knowledge and erudition. During the Shaoxing era, he first took charge of Lushan in Cixi.
He deeply detested those presiding over monastic communities who pre-emptively prepared burial vaults for themselves, often saying: "The mountain forests are finite, yet human remains are infinite;
as the years accumulate, there will eventually be no space left to contain them. He therefore established a cloister for three pagodas.
The ground was excavated to form a hollow, both deep and wide. It was covered with solid, polished stone and a stūpa was erected above it.
Within it, a niche for the Buddha rises high, while a small hole at its base leads secretly into the hollow.

Whenever a presiding monk passes away, after his cremation, his bones and *śarīra* relics are collected and passed through the small hole into the hollow. The second [monk] does likewise; the first...

He established this provision for the bhikṣus to eliminate their hunger, intending it as a means to accommodate donors; he wished that those who offered their support, regardless of their status, might be permitted to partake.
He inscribed a notice titled "The Three Pagodas," and all who heard of or saw it were moved by its excellence, for his intention was to inspire them deeply.

Not long after, while residing at Shitian Temple, he personally went to the southern corner of the temple, to the right of a vegetable garden, where he constructed over a hundred rooms. In the center...
The stupa of Kan Shou is protected by a balustrade and adorned with azure-green decorations. Pools and pavilions flank it, named "Cloud-Storing" and "Moon-Occupying.

Furthermore, he once disparaged the lack of majesty in the river valley and its foothills, moving the site three times. A passerby remarked, "Is this the same rusticity as that of Mount Lu in the past?
Is it not? Why was it excellent in the past but deficient now? I have heard that when one is poor, one must maintain integrity.

A covenant. To be arrogant and extravagant when wealthy, yet unable to be moved by poverty or wealth—this is what constitutes attaining it. When Lu Yao was as rich as Heaven, how could he have been moved from his attainment?
Huichun said of the lake: "In general, when composing works or engaging in debate, if one desires public clarity and correctness, one must be without personal bias."

How can you find peace in this? Do not concern yourself with such distress. The public verdict says: "The peach and plum trees do not speak, yet paths form beneath them of their own accord."

The intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is that each person should realize it for themselves.

Awaken to yourself; thus one is liberated from birth and death. Fundamentally, there is not a single dharma, yet there is the mutual transmission and reception that constitutes the relationship of teacher and disciple.

As my late master said: "The Way must be attained by oneself. To attain it is not to attain anything at all. When one wondrously accords with original emptiness, one possesses the wisdom of no-teacher and natural wisdom.
Even if you were to say, "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored," you would still be merely a person repeating the words of others.
The Great Man acts as the teacher of the primordial source; he possesses the function of the total mechanism. Therefore it is said:

"I am the Dharma King, sovereign over all dharmas. How could there be any restriction regarding lineage of transmission? What we now call "lineage of transmission" necessarily involves one who has first awakened awakening those who have not yet awakened;
thus, out of necessity, the titles of "teacher" and "disciple" came into being. Alas! The Dharma-ending age is gradually declining and differs vastly from antiquity.
Today’s masters do not inquire whether a candidate is fit or unfit; they habitually accept and nurture them with compassion.

They probe under the armpits to extract feathers, thinking to themselves that their lineage is flourishing and that they have many dharma heirs and disciples. They say, "This person has been among the assembly for many years;
upon meeting the master, he felt like casting off a heavy burden or shedding a foul cloak. He celebrates his entire life as having fully attained the Way of the Master, his intent being to...
They merely lend their names to others, seeking only personal gain. Alas, how tragic!
With the great masters of the past gone, if such practices continue, how much longer can the Buddha-dharma avoid sinking into oblivion?
In the *Dingwan*, it says: "Heaven is called the Father; Earth is called the Mother. I, who am so humble, dwell in the midst of them in a state of total integration.

Therefore, the vital essence of Heaven and Earth constitutes my body, and the commanding force of Heaven and Earth constitutes my nature. All people are my brothers; all things are my companions. The Public Critique (*Gonglun*) states:
"The single character 'se' (vital essence) seems like lifting Mount Tai and leaping across the North Sea; one exerts great effort and achieves great merit."
Gao Zhao, the Dharma Master, said: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one body with me.
The character "I" (吾) already requires too much mental exertion.

In his *Beishu* (Letter to the Heir Apparent), he asked: "In the investigation of things (*gewu*), must one investigate every single thing? Or is it sufficient to investigate a single thing so that all principles are thereby understood?"
[Zhang] Zhi asked, "How can one achieve such thorough penetration? If merely by investigating one thing one were to penetrate all principles, even Yanzi would not dare to speak thus.
One must investigate one thing today and another thing tomorrow;
once this practice has accumulated over time, one will then suddenly experience a spontaneous and thorough penetration. Gong Lun remarked, "Alas! This is the learning of the Cheng family."

Today I have seen it; thus I know that all the principles of human nature and phenomena I previously discussed were merely the harmonious integration of accumulated habits, entirely lacking anything attained through self-realization.
This was not the Way of true attainment.

When talent surpasses virtue, one is a petty person (*xiǎnrén*). When virtue surpasses talent, one is a gentleman (*jūnzǐ*). When both talent and virtue are superior, one is called a sage (*shèng rén*).
When both talent and virtue are absent, one is called a fool (*yúrén*). It would be better to be a fool than to be a petty person. How profound these words are!
They may truly be called the public judgment of the world.
Impartiality gives rise to clarity; partiality gives rise to darkness. If one harbors even a hair’s breadth of private interest, one will lack clarity; how, then, can one attain impartiality?

What I have discussed here—from the deliberations with my friends to the inquiries of juniors—is based on what has been verified by my own ears and eyes, attested within myself, and confirmed by the Way.

It is not by means of private likes and dislikes that one excludes or accepts, nor is it by contending for skill or peddling empty fame in the world of men that one transmits [the Dharma] to disciples, hoping they might become good people, gentlemen, or those who have attained the Way. Before he had finished speaking, a guest said:
"A person who has truly attained the Way does not see the faults of the world; yet the public consensus of the monastic communities (*conglin*) often favors those who are merely talkative."
"Why is this not considered 'exposure'? Meng said, "There is indeed such a saying. The Analects states: 'To loathe the act of exposing others as being straightforward.

Yet when Confucius composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, rebellious ministers and treacherous sons were struck with fear. Was that not also exposure? What we are discussing now is nothing other than this:
to rectify the deviant and clarify the correct; to cause those who are ignorant to understand. Thus, each may follow their own fundamental nature. Do you, my guest, consider this so?"
This concludes the "Public Discourse of the Forests" (Conglin Gonglun). No further discussion shall be pursued.
